title: ICC: The temporal vs the strategic
primary_topics: July 18 ICC Appeals Chamber 3-2 decision authorizing prosecutor Karim Khan to resume PH drug-war investigation
Two issues on appeal: complementarity (Article 17) and jurisdiction
Why the 3-judge majority skirted the jurisdiction question on procedural grounds (alleged waiver)
Why the 2-judge minority would have ruled on jurisdiction and dismissed for lack of it
CJ's framing: 'temporal' prosecutorial victory vs 'strategic' PH-government victory in knowing two judges already lean toward dismissal
sub_topics: Bensouda's Feb. 8, 2018 announcement of preliminary 'examination' of the PH situation
PH withdrawal from ICC on March 17, 2018; effective one year later on March 17, 2019
May 24, 2021 Bensouda PTC request (more than two years after effective withdrawal)
Sept. 15, 2021 PTC grant of authority to commence preliminary investigation
Khan agreed to suspend investigation at PH government's request
Jan. 26, 2023 PTC grant for Khan to continue (because government inquiry deemed 'allegedly superficial')
Article 17 Statute: ICC declines case if a State 'unwilling or unable genuinely to carry out' investigation

AC majority of three: PH failed to show genuine willingness/ability; alleged jurisdictional lack should have been raised in appeal of Sept. 15, 2021 decision (not Jan. 26, 2023); PH waived right by appealing only the latter
AC minority of two: refusal to take up jurisdiction was error; perpetrators could raise it later anyway when warrants issue; wasted time and resources to proceed without ruling
Minority's core jurisdictional argument: Bensouda's PTC petition was filed May 24, 2021 and granted Sept. 15, 2021 -- both more than two years past the March 17, 2019 effective withdrawal
Khan's silence and inaction since the AC ruling -- has he changed his mind given the minority's persuasive opinion?
Prosecutor's strategic calculation: better to redirect effort to clearer 'situations' like Russia's war on Ukraine
Core statutory-construction question: Is the Office of the Prosecutor an integral part of the ICC? CJ's short answer: No.

people: Karim Khan (ICC chief prosecutor, KC/Queen's Counsel)
events: March 17, 2018 PH submission of ICC withdrawal
March 17, 2019 effective date of PH withdrawal
Jan. 26, 2023 PTC grant for Khan to continue
July 18, 2023 AC 3-2 decision authorizing Khan to resume
Russia's war on Ukraine (referenced as alternative ICC situation)

stances.claim: On complementarity (Article 17), the AC correctly found that the PH government had not shown genuine willingness and ability to investigate the situation and prosecute the perpetrators 'especially the brains' of the alleged crime -- agreeing with Khan.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-acknowledgement of the AC majority's complementarity holding

stances.claim: On jurisdiction, the AC majority of three improperly skirted the issue on procedural grounds -- claiming the PH should have appealed the Sept. 15, 2021 decision (not the Jan. 26, 2023 one) and had thereby 'waived' its right to challenge jurisdiction.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-skepticism (the AC's procedural-waiver theory is questionable)

stances.claim: The two-judge minority got it right: jurisdiction will inevitably resurface when Khan seeks warrants, so refusing to rule now produces only wasted time and resources -- and the ICC did not acquire jurisdiction because Bensouda's PTC petition was filed and granted more than two years past the March 17, 2019 effective withdrawal.

Khan's victory is 'temporary' because the ICC may dismiss the complaints or warrant petitions for lack of jurisdiction once he files them -- and Khan may not pursue the case knowing his effort could be wasted, better redirected to new 'situations' like Russia's war on Ukraine.
stances.rhetorical_move: temporal-vs-strategic binary framing with prosecutorial-calculus prediction

stances.claim: The PH government, though it 'suffered a temporary defeat,' may have won 'strategic knowledge' -- at least two ICC judges are minded to dismiss, and notably no judge (including the three majority) has taken an opposing stance on the jurisdiction issue.
stances.rhetorical_move: strategic-knowledge framing (defeat in form, win in substance)

stances.claim: The jurisdiction question hinges on a single statutory-construction issue: Is the Office of the Prosecutor an integral part of the ICC for purposes of the Article 127 'already under consideration' exception? CJ's short answer: No.
stances.rhetorical_move: statutory-construction reduction (the whole controversy collapses to one yes/no question)

notable_anecdotes: Karim Khan introduced as 'a celebrated Queen's Counsel in the United Kingdom' -- a credentialing flourish that highlights the prosecutor's prestige even as CJ critiques his procedural posture.
Date-by-date chronological reconstruction with the explicit instruction 'Please note the dates carefully' -- turning the column into a teaching exercise on jurisdictional-timing arithmetic.
The 3-2 AC split: majority of three skirted jurisdiction on alleged waiver; minority of two would have tackled it and dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

CJ's prosecutorial-calculus speculation: Khan's silence and inaction since the AC ruling may reflect his strategic decision to redirect to clearer cases like Russia/Ukraine rather than press a possibly losing PH case.

Strategic-knowledge framing: 'at least two ICC judges are minded to dismiss the suit while none, not even any of the three majority judges, has taken an opposing stance on the vital issue of jurisdiction' -- a count of expressed positions, not just votes.

Closing reduction of the entire controversy to one question: 'Is the Office of the Prosecutor an integral part of the ICC? My short answer is No.' -- the same question A99 will pick up the following Monday.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the July 18 ICC Appeals Chamber 3-2 decision authorizing chief prosecutor Karim Khan -- 'a celebrated Queen's Counsel in the United Kingdom' -- to resume his investigation of the alleged 'crime against humanity of murder, committed in the Philippines between Nov. 1, 2011, and March 16, 2019, in the context of the so-called war on drugs.' He walks the reader carefully through the date chronology: Bensouda's Feb. 8, 2018 preliminary 'examination' announcement; PH withdrawal submitted March 17, 2018, effective March 17, 2019; Bensouda's PTC request only on May 24, 2021 (more than two years past effective withdrawal); PTC grant on Sept. 15, 2021; Khan's agreement to suspend at the PH government's request; PTC's Jan. 26, 2023 grant for Khan to continue because the government's inquiry was deemed 'allegedly superficial.' On appeal, the AC took up two issues: complementarity (where the majority agreed with Khan that the PH had not shown genuine willingness/ability under Article 17) and jurisdiction (which the majority skirted, claiming the PH waived the issue by appealing only the Jan. 26, 2023 decision instead of the underlying Sept. 15, 2021 one). The two-judge minority asserted this was error -- jurisdiction will resurface when warrants are sought, so refusing to rule now wastes resources -- and held that the ICC did not acquire jurisdiction because Bensouda's PTC petition was both filed and granted more than two years after effective withdrawal. CJ reads Khan's silence and inaction since the AC ruling as possibly meaning he 'may no longer be minded to pursue the case,' redirecting effort to clearer 'situations' like Russia's war on Ukraine. The PH government's strategic knowledge: two ICC judges are minded to dismiss, and notably no judge has taken an opposing stance on jurisdiction. CJ closes by reducing the whole controversy to one statutory-construction question -- 'Is the Office of the Prosecutor an integral part of the ICC?' -- and answers, 'My short answer is No.'
